default.p.test-11-p1.vietnamese:
I think there are quite a few things we cannot throw away because we believe we might use them someday. Ironically, however, the day when we need the very things we think this way about never seems to come. When we decisively throw things away or reduce the number of items in our room, our mood becomes surprisingly lighter and more refreshed. First, before throwing anything away, we must decide, “I will throw this away.” In fact, this determination itself has a positive effect on our mental state. If the state of not knowing what to do and being unable to make a decision continues, the mind gradually loses its vitality and becomes exhausted. By making decisions, we also organize our thoughts and feel more refreshed and comfortable. In addition, this can improve our ability to make decisions.

Having too many possessions also causes considerable stress. The more we have—not only physical objects, but also information and choices—the more troubled and anxious we become. People have always worked hard to increase their wealth and options, but could that not be precisely why modern society is called a stressful society? Having nothing, by contrast, can make us feel more comfortable and relieved.

Those who feel it is a waste to throw things away can give them to someone else or sell them. If you inexplicably feel low on energy, irritated, or restless, try thoroughly cleaning your room and reducing your possessions. It may do you good.

default.p.test-12-p1.vietnamese:
At a busy train station, I noticed a foreign traveler carrying a large suitcase. Seeing the person holding a travel guide and looking very anxious, I instinctively asked in English, "Are you having any trouble?"

"How can I get to the platform for Kyoto?"

"Oh, in that case, it must be platform 8."

As soon as I said this, I thought to myself: "I wonder if they will be all right. They are in a foreign country and do not speak Japanese. This place is crowded, so they might get lost. Maybe I should guide them part of the way." With that thought, I said, "Then please follow me." I could understand English at about this level, at least to some extent.

When you are in trouble, it is truly comforting to be treated kindly by someone else. I have had a similar experience myself. I remembered the kind woman who helped me, even though I could not speak the language, when I was lost in the countryside of Italy and could not find either a bus or a taxi. Wondering whether I had managed to do something kind for someone else, as that woman had done for me, I returned home in a very pleasant mood.

default.p.test-13-p1.vietnamese:
People seem to become more motivated to work harder when they are praised or when others have high expectations of them. This is probably true in child-rearing, school education, and the workplace as well.

The phenomenon in which a person’s actual abilities improve when others believe that “this child can surely do it” and place expectations on them is called the “Pygmalion effect.” Expectations and praise awaken a person’s own “motivation.” For example, mothers of young children may be asked questions such as, “At about what age do you normally think children can put on their shoes by themselves?” or “At about what age do you think children can dress themselves?” It has been found that the children of mothers who believe their children will be able to do these things at an earlier age than other mothers tend, in fact, to become able to do them at a very early age. This could perhaps also be called the “Pygmalion effect.”

Whether excessive expectations or praise, to the point that they become a burden, should be avoided is something that must be considered. Nevertheless, is this not a term that teaches us the importance of believing that others have potential and expecting great things from them, rather than labeling them as “hopeless anyway”?

(Note 1) Phenomenon: An observed fact

(Note 2) Young child: A small child

(Note 3) Burden: Something that feels heavy or difficult to bear

(Note 4) Have potential: To have hope or promise

default.p.test-14-p1.vietnamese:
When we sleep well, we feel relaxed and the day's work progresses smoothly. Conversely, when we do not sleep well, our ability to think declines, our spirits become sluggish and lifeless, and we may feel irritated and cranky all day. For this reason, good sleep is indispensable to our lives.

If we describe specifically what good sleep is like, the first condition is being able to fall asleep as soon as we get into bed. Everyone becomes frustrated when they intend to sleep but cannot fall asleep for a long time. Next, we should not wake up in the middle of the night. Waking up at midnight and going back to sleep—the so-called "second sleep-in"—does not leave us feeling refreshed. I think everyone has experienced the joy of waking up and realizing there is still time to sleep, but in fact that is not a state of having slept well at all. Is it not also often the case that going back to sleep ultimately makes us oversleep?

To sleep well, it is necessary to review our daily habits. We should avoid such things as eating, drinking, or playing games until just before bedtime. This is because our so-called biological clock has a major influence, rather than actual clock time alone. In addition, preparing the bedroom environment properly is another key point. Factors such as the brightness and sounds in the room, and the condition of the bedding, all affect sleep. Simply trying to forget the worries and stress of the day and consciously telling yourself that you will sleep deeply can also make a significant difference.

In response to the teacher's question, everyone's hand shot up.

"It's strange that only boys appear in video game commercials. Even I play them," a girl said.

"Families in commercials are always made up of a kind father and mother and adorable sons and daughters. What's more, everyone looks happy. But isn't that strange?" another girl asked.

By comparing "reality in the media" with "the reality in which they themselves live," the students reexamined in a fresh way the world reflected by the media. They learned that commercials are "created" to sell products, rather than being reality itself. They also learned that images such as "standard masculine and feminine characteristics" and "happy families," although they surround children, are not necessarily "the truth." The class gradually helped the children recognize these things.

We who live in Japan also go about our daily lives exposed to many different forms of media. Shouldn't we, in addition to learning to read and write and comprehend texts, also learn about the media?

(Note 1) Media: television, radio, newspapers, magazines, and so on

(Note 2) Commercial: here, an advertisement or promotional message broadcast on television

default.p.test-16-p1.vietnamese:
Today, I would like to introduce Mr. Matsuda, a former junior high school teacher who is now a university lecturer. When he was a junior high school teacher, Mr. Matsuda restored order to a school that had been thrown into chaos by bullying and led its baseball club to five national championships. Mr. Matsuda believes that developing "independent-minded people" is more important than anything else. The distinctive feature of his training method is that he first asks students to write down specific goals for themselves. With those goals in mind, he helps them clearly recognize their own problems and think of solutions on their own. In this way, cultivating people who can think and act for themselves is Mr. Matsuda’s style.

Mr. Matsuda also spoke about the relationship between superiors and subordinates in the workplace.

「Imagine that there is a river here. Crossing this river together—that is the relationship between a senior and a junior. The relationship between a superior and a subordinate, however, is different. The subordinate is on the opposite bank, and the superior must find a way to enable the subordinate to cross to this bank on their own. At that point, if the superior merely speaks gently and flatters the subordinate, it will not motivate the subordinate. If you truly want to improve a subordinate’s abilities, you must never be afraid of the opposition between the two banks of the river. To do that, while accurately assessing the subordinate’s abilities, the superior must also frankly point out the subordinate’s shortcomings.」

Mr. Matsuda says, "What is important for a leader is to always care about and stay connected with their employees, no matter what." "Praising them is fine, and scolding them is fine too. The essential thing is always to care about them and get involved with them. That is what matters." Whether it is adults raising children, teachers educating students, or superiors dealing with subordinates, the basic principle is the same.

default.p.test-17-p1.vietnamese:
A

When sushi is mentioned, it is now a dish enjoyed by people all over the world. However, looking at its history, it apparently took some time for sushi to gain worldwide acceptance. The reason is that people in countries without a tradition of eating raw fish were somewhat hesitant to try it. Therefore, when people began putting butter and smoked salmon inside instead of raw fish and selling it, the dish suited American tastes and became a major success. From then on, together with new dining styles such as conveyor-belt sushi, it gradually became a trend. In any form, it is truly delightful to see a dish from one's own country enjoyed by people all over the world. Perhaps one day even umeboshi, which is currently criticized as 「too sour to eat!」, will attract the attention of people around the world.

B

On February 1, an instant food called 「stir-fried chicken tteokbokki」 went on sale nationwide. Although it had already been popular among Japanese people interested in Korea, this was the first time that tteokbokki that was not imported had been sold in Japanese supermarkets. Since last year, young people in Japan have rapidly developed an intense interest in Korean television dramas and songs, and Korean food culture also seems to be gradually spreading in Japan. Around the world, countless dishes that are not yet widely known remain undiscovered. I hope that people will continue actively searching for and introducing more and more foods that suit Japanese tastes.

default.p.test-18-p1.outline.1.label: A: Negative effects of cram schools on students
default.p.test-18-p1.outline.1.note: Author A points out that students demand “customer service” at school as though it were a cram school, and criticizes juku for taking away students’ ability to think independently and ask their own questions. This supports questions 1 and 2.
default.p.test-18-p1.outline.2.label: B — The classroom situation at school and the problem of students falling behind

default.p.test-18-p1.outline.3.label: B — The positive role of cram schools and proposals for regular schools

default.p.test-18-p1.vietnamese:
A

When children reach around junior high school age, the number of students attending cram school begins to increase. The purpose is to improve their understanding of school lessons and raise their academic performance through supplementary study.

However, cram schools in recent years have begun to directly affect students' attitudes toward school. Students unintentionally bring to school the same level of service they receive as “customers” at cram school and demand it from their schools.

For example, if students cannot ask questions or look things up on their own when they do not understand something in class, they will be unable to keep up with school education. Yet some students complain to the school, thinking, “I would understand if the teacher explained things carefully to each student, but the teacher does not, so I hate it and refuse to cooperate.” Of course, the teachers' teaching methods may also have problems. However, I believe the more serious problem is that cram schools teach students methods for raising their scores from A to Z rather than methods of learning, depriving them of the ability to think and ask questions for themselves.

B

In the past, elementary school classes often had around 50 students. Today, however, due to the declining birth rate, there are reportedly many places with fewer than 20 students per class. Nevertheless, it would be wrong to say that teachers' burden has been reduced as a result. At quite a few schools, lessons cannot proceed at all because students “will not sit in their seats.” In such circumstances, what students learn in class naturally fails to sink in, and some students fall behind. That is why the vast majority of students turn to cram schools. Recently, cram schools have gradually become like a second school: teachers there listen to students' concerns about school, and some even organize field trips. Students who have fallen behind in school education are brought back to life there. The difference from regular schools probably lies in more than simply the atmosphere of the buildings. Shouldn't schools recognize this, stop treating cram schools as enemies, and show a willingness to learn from what they do well?

(Note 1) Ochikobore: Here, students who cannot keep up with lessons in class

(Note 2) Iki o fukikaesu: Something that seemed about to fail or collapse recovers and comes back to life.

default.p.test-19-p1.vietnamese:
A person seeking advice

I am currently studying abroad at a language school in the United States. I have been preparing to enter university in the spring, but I heard from Japan last week that my father said it might be difficult to pay my university tuition. When I heard this, I considered giving up, but I truly still want to work part-time and somehow manage on my own. However, I also think that unless I find an exceptionally good part-time job, it will probably be very difficult to cover both living expenses and tuition while studying. Therefore, any useful information would be appreciated, whether it concerns how to find a part-time job with good conditions or inexpensive apartments.

Respondent A

I do understand that you do not want to return home, but if you can speak English, wouldn't it be easier to find a part-time job with good conditions in Japan? I think having to earn both your tuition and living expenses yourself will be far more difficult than you imagine. It is entirely possible that you may become so absorbed in your part-time job that you neglect your studies. Wouldn't it be better to work part-time in Japan, save enough for your tuition and living expenses, and then study abroad again? It would not be too late.

Respondent B

You may already have looked into it, but what about scholarships? Although it depends on the type of scholarship, some provide full tuition coverage to outstanding students. If you received one, wouldn't you only need to work part-time to cover your living expenses? For your reference, I would like to introduce a few websites related to scholarships in the United States. Although they concern the United States, it is a very large country, so I do not know whether they contain information about the university or area you are interested in. Still, please take a look.
http://www.scholarship.xx.yy
http://www.studysupport.xx.yy

default.p.test-20-p1.vietnamese:
Everyone knows that consuming plenty of calcium is good for building strong bones. However, fewer people know that exercise is equally important. If a person does not exercise enough during childhood, their bones are more likely to break in old age, and they may develop a condition called osteoporosis.

Although exercise is important, that does not mean every type of exercise is beneficial. Activities such as dancing, jogging, and high jumping are effective for building strong bones, whereas swimming is considered to have little effect. Exercises that support one's own body weight while being performed are very useful for strengthening bones. However, because the human body floats on water, this need does not exist in the water.

Exercise has many different benefits, and suitable exercises make bones larger and stronger. In addition, the muscles surrounding the bones become stronger, and those muscles help maintain bone strength. Furthermore, people who exercise regularly can move their bodies more quickly in response to danger, making them less likely than people who do not exercise at all to suffer fractures or injuries in accidents.

Exercise for general health is beneficial at any stage of life, but exercise to build strong bones is different. This is because the skeleton is completed and takes its final shape between birth and around the age of 30. Considering this, we can understand that it is best to build a strong skeleton from childhood. To build strong bones, it is extremely important to perform effective exercises at the appropriate time.

(Note 1) Osteoporosis: A disease that causes the bones to become fragile and weak

(Note 2) Appropriate (適切な): Suitable, at the right level (ちょうどいい)

default.p.test-21-p1.vietnamese:
This time, we spoke with Mitsuo Tanaka, the director who recently founded a job-placement company for foreign nationals.

Question: What exactly does your company do?

Answer: We currently have more than 1,400 registered people. Put simply, our job is to introduce them to companies that match their preferences as closely as possible. In other words, we say, "We have a foreign national who can do this kind of work. Would your company be able to hire them?" Of course, companies also contact us and say, "We want to hire a foreign national with these qualifications. Can you introduce us to a suitable person?" In short, we serve as a bridge connecting foreign nationals and businesses.

Question: I see. But the economy has been weak lately. Has that made things very difficult?

Answer: Yes. Even Japanese people find it difficult to secure a good job, so it is even more difficult for foreign nationals. Only about 5% of those who register actually end up being hired.

Question: What advice would you give to foreign nationals who hope to find work in Japan in the future?

Answer: Let me see. I would like you to develop communication skills sufficient to travel with Japanese people. In particular, what I want to tell international students is that more concerning than their knowledge of honorific language or vocabulary is their lack of experience interacting with Japanese people. Even if you use a word incorrectly, people will understand because you are, after all, a foreign national. The same applies to honorific language: as long as you use the 「desu / masu」 form and speak without being rude, there is no problem at all. However, if you lack skills such as knowing how to choose a topic of conversation, how to use aizuchi, or how to sense the atmosphere of the place, you will encounter considerable confusion and trouble when working with Japanese people. In addition, it is probably important to take an active interest in Japanese culture.

（Note 1）不景気: A condition in which the economy of society is poor.

（Note 2）就職: Obtaining and beginning a job.

default.p.test-22-p1.vietnamese:
“When I was in school, I was very good at math, so I thought I was the type of person with a talent for mathematics, but……”

“As for me, I was completely terrible at math from my school days and had no talent at all. I worry about whether this will be passed on to my son……”

I often hear stories like these. Many people discuss whether someone has a talent for mathematics based on their math test scores at school. However, from elementary-school arithmetic to understanding university-level mathematics, talent or anything similar has nothing to do with it. ① The ability to understand it is not very different from the ability to live an ordinary daily life. That is what I think. The ability worthy of being called ② “a talent for mathematics” refers to that possessed by great mathematicians who make their mark on history, and my view is that there is only one such person every hundred years or so.

So what kind of ability is “the ability to understand university-level mathematics,” or “the ability to live an ordinary daily life”?

Perhaps we only need to regard it as the ability to do the following four things. If someone can do these things, the rest depends on effort. The four things are: “being able to look up a word in a dictionary,” “being able to put one’s schoolbag in the correct locker,” “being able to cook,” and “being able to draw a map.” Why can we say that having these abilities means someone can understand university-level mathematics?

For example, being able to “look up a word in an English dictionary” means being able to understand the order of the 26 letters of the alphabet. With a Japanese dictionary, it means being able to understand the relative order of 51 characters. Being able to “use one’s locker” means being able to put one’s schoolbag in the locker bearing one’s own number—in other words, understanding one-to-one correspondence. Being able to “cook” means having the ability to observe things and make predictions, while being able to “draw a map” means having the ability to use lines and symbols to convert real space into a flat surface—in other words, the ability to abstract.

Therefore, I believe that people who possess all four of these abilities but still cannot learn mathematics do not lack the ability to understand mathematics; they are simply unwilling to make the effort and have become lazy.

◆ Maruiya Supermarket will open in front of Sakura Station on Monday, March 1!

◆ Would you like to start a part-time job together at the newly opened supermarket?
Those interested are encouraged to apply actively.

【Qualifications】 Men and women aged 18 or over
【Applying】 Please contact us by phone first. When you do so, be sure to tell us which part-time position you wish to apply for.
Interviews will be held from Monday, February 8, through Friday, February 12.
For the interview, attach a photograph to your résumé and bring it with you.
Contact: 03-3333-222X　Person in charge: Sato (さとう)

【Application deadline】 Applications will be accepted through Wednesday, January 20.

＊ The cashier, bakery, and laundry positions are looking for people who can work at least 3 days a week.

Alan, a 23-year-old international student, is studying at Sakura Japanese Language School and plans to work part-time when he has no classes. 【Procedures for Using the Conference Room at the Research Exchange Center】

1. Eligible users
1）Officers and employees of research institutions in Yamada City
2）Officers and employees of research institutions outside Yamada City who conduct research exchanges with the officers and employees mentioned above
3）Persons deemed eligible by the Director of the Research Exchange Center

2. Usage fee
Free of charge

3. Usage days and hours
Weekdays (Monday–Friday) / 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
※ The facility may be entered from 8:30 a.m. for preparation and other purposes.
After the conference, please return the room to its original condition and leave before 5:00 p.m.

4. Application procedure
After confirming room availability by telephone, please complete the required items on the application form and submit it together with documents related to the conference.
〔Start of application period〕 In principle, applications are accepted starting three months before the conference date.

5. Submission of the application
〔Application method〕 Applications are accepted by FAX or e-mail.
〔Application office〕 First-floor office of the Research Exchange Center

6. Issuance of the usage permit
After confirming the application details and other information, we will issue a usage permit.
Please present the usage permit at the reception desk on the day of use.

【Facilities and Equipment】
・Food and beverage facilities: None.
※ Eating, drinking, and smoking inside the conference room are prohibited.
Please eat, drink, and smoke in designated areas.
・Vending machines: First and second floors
・Coin-operated lockers (free): Second floor (30 compartments)
・Internet access: Internet access is available through the LAN equipment installed in the conference room.
※ Please bring your own computer, LAN card, and LAN cable.

【Parking】 Capacity: 70 vehicles ※ If the parking lot is full, please use nearby paid parking lots.
【Contact】 TEL: 0436-22-1111 FAX: 0436-22-1122 E-mail: info@yamadakenkyu.com

default.p.test-26-p1.sentences.2.keys.0.why: Few people think their recorded voice sounds better than the voice they hear themselves, confirming that most people find the recorded voice worse.
default.p.test-26-p1.sentences.3.vi: This can be described as a phenomenon similar to the fact that many people look at themselves in a photograph and refuse to accept their appearance, asking, 「これがわたし？」.

default.p.test-26-p1.sentences.3.keys.0.why: Similar to hearing one’s recorded voice, many people look at photographs of themselves but refuse to accept their appearance because they feel they look worse in the picture than in reality. Together, these points support choice 4: both their voice and image seem worse than they really are.
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.0.label: Failing to recognize one’s own voice when hearing a recording.
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.0.note: Begins with a common phenomenon: when people hear a recording of their own voice, almost no one thinks it sounds like them.
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.1.label: The tendency to judge recorded voices as worse than they really are
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.1.note: The passage analyzes the majority’s psychology: people think their real voice must sound better, or less unpleasant, and very few feel that their recorded voice sounds better than the voice they hear themselves. This supports question 1.
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.2.label: The similarity to the psychology of seeing oneself in photographs
default.p.test-26-p1.outline.2.note: The author expands the discussion and concludes that hearing one's recorded voice is similar to looking at a photograph and refusing to accept one's appearance because it seems worse than reality. This further supports Question 1.
default.p.test-26-p1.vietnamese: People often say: 「When we hear a recording of our own voice, we cannot believe it is our voice」. Many people apparently think: 「My voice isn't really this bad. It must be better than this」. Very few people seem to think that 「my recorded voice」 is better than 「the voice I think of as my own」. This can be said to be a phenomenon similar to how many people see themselves in a photograph, refuse to accept their appearance, and wonder 「Is this really me?」.

The following is an email sent to members by a civic club.

Thank you very much to everyone who came in such large numbers yesterday to Sakura Civic Hall despite the rain and difficult road conditions. Thanks to you, the seminar commemorating our third anniversary ended successfully and was a great success. Once again, we would like to express our deepest gratitude.

After the seminar, we received many inquiries asking whether the seminar materials (the PowerPoint presentation and handouts) could be provided as files. We also realized that this would be useful for members who were unable to attend this time, so today we have decided to send the materials by email. Please download them from the attachment and make good use of them.

In addition, regarding the notice for the next regular meeting, we will contact you again in the next few days. We hope that you will continue to invite others and join us in large numbers next time.

We are sending this brief message both to thank you and to provide you with an update.

Association for Reflecting on Multicultural Coexistence

Representative: Hitomi Yamada

default.p.test-30-p1.vietnamese: Because many companies sent emails saying things like, “We regret to inform you that you were not selected. We sincerely wish you every success in the future,” students began calling rejection emails “Oinori mail” (“prayer-for-your-success mail”). When a company sends no notice at all and the applicant is rejected without realizing when it happened, this is called “Silent oinori” (“silent rejection”). With “Oinori mail,” students can pull themselves together and continue applying to other companies, but “Silent oinori” makes that impossible. Among students, there is overwhelming support for the view that companies should stop silently rejecting applicants. Staff at university career-support centers also agree, saying, “We strongly hope that companies will always notify applicants of the selection results.”

default.p.test-31-p1.vietnamese:
A Korean proverb says, 「A thief who studies late does not realize that dawn has broken」.

Its meaning seems to be that, whatever the activity, people who begin it later in life are very likely to become deeply absorbed in it.

I think it corresponds to the Japanese expression 「An affair after forty cannot be stopped」, but compared with the metaphor of an affair, the humorous image of a late-learning thief becoming so absorbed that he keeps fiddling with a lock or rustling around in a storeroom until someone discovers him at dawn is much more amusing.

It also seems to contain the teasing implication of 「An old person drinking cold water」. Every time I remember this proverb, I find it amusing and instinctively connect it with, and superimpose it on, my own present self.

That is because, after passing the age of fifty, I began studying the Hangul script of a neighboring country, and before I knew it, ten years had passed. ①I truly am a late-learning thief.

Sometimes I become so absorbed in the enjoyment that I do not notice dawn beginning to break, but in language study it is certainly fortunate not to hear someone shout 「Stop!」 or 「You are under arrest!」. If I had been younger, I might have studied more quickly and skillfully, whereas after turning fifty, I inevitably need several times more time and effort.

Nevertheless, deep down, I also quietly think ②as follows. When we are young, our command of the context and textual foundations of Japanese is not yet secure. After passing fifty, one could say that we have nearly mastered Japanese. After that, it is not too late to leisurely embark on a 「journey into a foreign language」.

③Studying a foreign language is also a matter of one's native language. Many young people speak foreign languages fluently, yet their Japanese is halting and awkward.

(Note 1) 暁時: the time when night is about to turn into dawn

(Note 2) 御用: an expression said to have been used by Edo-period officials when arresting criminals

(Note 3) お縄頂戴: an expression said to have been used by Edo-period officials when arresting and tying criminals with rope

default.p.test-32-p1.vietnamese:
I have previously explained that Japanese is systemically isolated. At present, it can be understood as being separated from the world's other languages. So, is Japanese a peculiar, strange language with characteristics completely different from those of other languages? Many speculations and discussions about the uniqueness of Japanese have emerged over the years. Eventually, even seemingly plausible theories appeared, such as “That is precisely why Japanese people are poor at foreign languages.” Based on this premise, the argument developed further: unlike English, the reason the number of foreigners who become proficient in Japanese does not continue to increase is that Japanese is inherently unique and difficult as a language. But what is the truth?

According to experts familiar with many languages, if we examine each characteristic with an open-minded perspective, the truth seems to be that Japanese is not nearly as unique as people claim. In terms of pronunciation, such as the number of vowels and the nature of its consonants, Japanese is said to be fairly average—or, more accurately, close to the standard.

The features regarded as characteristic of Japanese grammar may include the lack of articles, the absence of a singular–plural distinction, the lack of relative pronouns, the fact that the subject is not obligatory, the fact that word order is not Subject–Verb–Object but places the predicate at the end of the sentence, and the way multiple elements are combined with a verb to form a predicate—for example, changing "食べる" into "食べさせられていなかったようだね". However, if we think about it carefully, aren't most of these features simply made noticeable because they differ from English—the first foreign language to which most Japanese people are exposed? Using English as the standard for foreign languages is an entirely different issue from the characteristics of English as a language.

default.p.test-33-p1.outline.0.label: The number of celestial bodies and the conditions necessary for life to arise
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the planets and satellites in the Solar System and raises the question of what conditions are necessary for life to form.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.1.label: Condition 1: A heavy element appears on the surface
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.1.note: Heavy elements essential for life (C, O, etc.) must be exposed on the rocky surface rather than enclosed in hydrogen and helium gas as they are on Jupiter and Saturn. This provides the basis for Question 1.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.2.label: Condition 2: weathering of soil and rock through water and the atmosphere
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.2.note: Rocks and soil must weather into gases and dust so that their elements can react to form compounds; this process requires water and an atmosphere. The basis for Question 2 is here.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.3.label: The key role of liquid water in chemical reactions
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.3.note: Emphasizes that liquid water is indispensable because it dissolves elements and accelerates chemical reactions. Provides additional evidence for Question 2.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.4.label: Water's effects in regulating temperature and purifying the atmosphere
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.4.note: Circulating water regulates temperature, like an air conditioner, and absorbs CO2; the author asserts that water is the key to creating life. Basis for Question 3.
default.p.test-33-p1.vietnamese:
There are 9 planets in the Solar System, and more than 90 satellites accompanying these planets in total.

For life to arise on these planets and satellites, several conditions must be met.

First, heavy elements such as carbon and oxygen, which are materials that make up life, must become part of the rocky material and be exposed on the surface. On giant planets such as Jupiter and Saturn, these elements are densely surrounded by gases consisting mainly of hydrogen and helium, so it is probably impossible for organic matter—compounds whose main component is carbon—to form.

Next, for heavy elements to react with one another and form compounds, rocks must undergo weathering and turn into gas or dust. This is because new compounds cannot form if the materials remain solid. For weathering to occur, atmospheres and water must exist on the surfaces of the planets and satellites.

In particular, liquid water is indispensable. This is because when various elements dissolve in water, chemical reactions proceed efficiently.

Furthermore, water undergoes a cycle: it absorbs energy from the ground, turns into water vapor, and rises; in the sky, it returns to liquid form, releases energy into outer space, and comes back to the ground.

In this way, water regulates the planet’s surface, preventing excessive heat by acting like an air conditioner, while also absorbing carbon dioxide, a type of “greenhouse gas,” and purifying the atmosphere. It can be said that the existence of water is the key to giving rise to life.

default.p.test-34-p1.vietnamese:
A

The "Three-Year-Old Myth" is the belief that "if a mother does not raise her child at home until the child turns three, it will cause irreparable harm to the child." Because it has not been scientifically proven, it is called a "myth." However, since many people believe in it, when a mother plans to send her child to a nursery school, people around her criticize her, saying, "If the mother does not raise the child herself until age three, the child will not grow up properly." This leads people to regard the mother as the only important person in the child's development, confining both mother and child to the family sphere.

B

There is a myth that "a mother should raise her child by her side until the child is three years old." The myth continues: "If she does not do so, it will negatively affect the child's development." This is almost a threat. Although the myth originated from observational and experimental reports, it has no scientific basis. However, it is difficult for nonspecialists to confidently declare that it is a lie. That is the problem.

When parents are subjected to this myth, they want to argue back: "Does that mean that all children raised in nursery schools turn out badly?" However, once negative effects occur, it is impossible to return to the time before the child turned three. Aren't many mothers feeling dissatisfied yet still being forced to obey this myth without question? Measures to prevent mothers from becoming isolated are eagerly awaited.

default.p.test-35-p1.vietnamese:
In the past, Japanese people used to regard having a hobby as a sin. Perhaps this was because they feared that people would become absorbed in pleasure and grow lazy about work or study.

On the other hand, people in the past also knew that human beings cannot go on living without pleasure.

For one person, pleasure may be reading; for another, sports, travel, or enjoying various forms of art. It varies greatly from person to person. For an office worker, fishing may be the greatest pleasure, whereas for a fisherman it is work, not a hobby. Some people enjoy assembling radios on their days off, while others assemble radios at a factory every day as their occupation.

When something becomes an occupation, it may still bring pleasure, but it also comes with hardship and worry.

I have loved Rakugo since I was a boy. I enjoyed listening to it, reading it, and even performing it myself. I also learned a great deal from this art. By devoting myself to it, I became able to appreciate the appeal of many other art forms as well.

However, after turning it into my profession, hardship and worry arose, and for a time I somewhat regretted having unintentionally transformed the Rakugo I had loved for so long into something that was no longer enjoyable. Yet after overcoming that period, I gradually came to understand aspects of the art and depths that I had never noticed before. Moreover, through Rakugo I was compelled to think deeply about what might be called a philosophy of life: how one should live as a human being, empathy and understanding of people's feelings, distinguishing right from wrong in matters of value, and many other such things.

Finally, I became able to confidently say something to my apprentices and junior colleagues.

I have just turned fifty. In the world of the arts, this is said to be the age when one is “only just beginning…” I may continue to change from now on, but at this point I have obtained permission to write this book. I am certain that I have not written a single dishonest or exaggerated thing in it. I devoted all my energy to writing it because I want people to understand what Rakugo is.

I have not written anything stiff or formal, so please feel free to read it.

default.p.test-36-p1.vietnamese:
Frequently Asked Questions and Answers about the「Kato City Civic Academy Foreign Language Course—Fall Term」

Q1. Is there a foreign language course that people who have never studied the language before can attend?

A1. The fall course (October ~ February) currently accepting applications is basically a continuation of the spring course (April ~ July). Since a beginner course such as「Beginner I」is offered every year in the spring, please consider enrolling from the next academic year.
※ However, depending on the language, a「Beginner」course may not be offered.

Q2. How many levels are the foreign language courses divided into?

A2. The Kato City Civic Academy foreign language courses have two levels,「Beginner」and「Pre-intermediate」. Depending on the language, there is also an「Intermediate」level to develop more advanced communication skills. In addition, some courses specialize in「Conversation」or「Reading Comprehension」.
（Reference guidelines for students at each level）
「Beginner」→ People studying the language for the first time
「Pre-intermediate」→ People who have studied the beginner level for one year, or whose language ability is considered sufficient to have mastered the beginner-level content
「Intermediate」→ People who have studied the beginner or pre-intermediate level for about two years, or whose language ability is equivalent to that level

Q3. Can I sit in on or try a class?

A3. Our academy does not offer class observation or trial lessons. Please read the enrollment information or website carefully and confirm the details. You can also view part of the textbook used in the course on the website, so please refer to it.

Q4. After the classes have started, can I change courses if I find that the level is not suitable?

A4. Unfortunately, courses cannot be changed after classes have started. We ask for your understanding and apologize for the inconvenience.

I have a friend who says that she cannot cook any dish without looking at a book. She says she has been married for 10 years and looks at a cookbook every day to prepare all three meals—breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Even when she eats out, she always reads a book such as「A Guide to Famous Restaurants」before going out. When buying clothes, she visits stores featured in magazines and buys exactly the outfits shown in the magazines.

Marusugi Industrial Company
Dear Mr. Ichiro Suzuki, Sales Department

We are always grateful for your company's support and kindness.
I am Kotaro Yamamoto from the Sales Department of HM Corporation.

Although you were very busy the other day, you took us on a tour of your factory, and we would like to express our sincere gratitude.
We all agreed that seeing your product assembly process was extremely meaningful for our work in the future.
We will likely ask your company for guidance on many matters from now on, and we hope that you will continue to advise and assist us when we do.
Although an email is somewhat inadequate, I would first like to express our sincere thanks.

HM Corporation
Sales Department
Kotaro Yamamoto

default.p.test-40-p1.vietnamese:
I had heard before that foreigners in Japan are not viewed very favorably in the real estate business. I heard that when Chinese people cook for themselves, they may be refused for reasons such as Chinese food being greasy and making the room dirty.

Several years ago, at the request of a professor, I helped find a place to rent for an international student from Yunnan. Feeling uneasy, I went from one real estate office to another. As expected, among the refusals were expressions such as 「for various reasons that are difficult to explain」 and 「we are afraid that it would be difficult for us to help you」. From a linguistic perspective, I was especially interested in the latter expression. At the same time, for some reason, I felt relieved and reassured. Compared with being told directly, 「We cannot help you,」 that wording feels much softer and more tactful.

default.p.test-41-p1.vietnamese:
People often ask me, "Isn't it better to start learning shogi when you are young?" (Some of the passage has been omitted.)

I am skeptical of the idea that "people improve more if they start when they are young." In any field, people who begin learning at an older age tend to rely more on knowledge than on instinct. However, that does not necessarily mean this is a disadvantage. In the world of shogi, the quality of play is constantly changing rapidly, and players will certainly reach times when they have to adjust their playing style. It is extremely difficult to replace a playing style learned instinctively in childhood with a new one. Since knowledge-based learning is easier to forget than instinctive learning, it also has the advantage of making it easier to accept the next new development. One can refresh one's own style and, in a sense, adapt more easily to progress and change.

default.p.test-42-p1.vietnamese:
When what we hear is new information—something we have never known before—we generally do not respond with 'Yes' (Hai). Instead, we use reactions such as 'Huh?', 'Oh, really?', 'I see', 'Really?', or 'No way!/You're kidding!'.

In the past, I heard an international student say that the expressions 'You're lying!?' and 'You're lying!' made them feel as though the other person regarded what they had said as a lie, which was rather uncomfortable. In English, for example, if someone suddenly responded to something perfectly ordinary that another person had said by saying, 'That's a lie!' it would certainly be rude.

However, the Japanese expressions 'You're lying!?' and 'You're lying!' are, in this respect, ways of expressing surprise. They originally carry a somewhat questioning implication, such as 'Really? You aren't lying, are you?' They can be said to signal that the information is new to the speaker—more precisely, that it is somewhat surprising information. They are perhaps used with a feeling similar to 'Really?' in English. The greater the surprise, the more valuable the information seems, so the expression becomes slightly exaggerated. Therefore, in the same situation, instead of 'You're lying!?' or 'You're lying!', one can also say 'Really!?'. When you think about it, 'true' and 'false' are complete opposites, so it is indeed strange. Still, when receiving new information, people use questioning expressions such as 'Is that true?' or 'You aren't lying, are you?' to seek confirmation.

Saying 'You're lying!?' or 'I can't believe it' expresses an even stronger degree of surprise.

default.p.test-43-p1.vietnamese:
I think that in any company, organization, or group, there are times when its members sit down together and talk about the organization itself. Some people make harsh comments about their superiors or colleagues, while others passionately express their visions and thoughts about how the organization needs to change.

Within these kinds of conversations, there are two directions in which the energy can move.

One is when the way of speaking becomes something like: “That person and that thing are no good. This company is bad in this area. It lacks this and that.” In this pattern, people protect themselves while attacking others, so the speakers themselves appear to be largely passive. They do not realize that they are blaming everything on other people, and they do not see themselves as positive, proactive agents.

The other direction is when the way of speaking becomes something like: “We need to make the organization like this. I want to guide the organization to develop in this direction.” In that case, the speakers themselves are largely proactive.

Although the content of the conversations may be similar, the direction of the energy is different in each case. Because proactive speakers have a sense of being involved, they may possess an inner strength capable of influencing the organization and the people around them. People like this have the potential to become those who drive organizational reform—in other words, change agents, or messengers who promote innovation.

default.p.test-44-p1.vietnamese:
After noon, I proudly told my husband, "I found a 1,000-yen bill early this morning. What do you think?" His expression suddenly darkened, and he became gloomy. "I dropped a one-yen coin in the station restroom, and although it looked dirty, I picked it up reflexively..." The reason my husband was so depressed that his shoulders drooped was that there is a theory that says, "The energy spent picking up a dropped one-yen coin costs more than one yen." In other words, suppose you see one yen. The energy used to transmit a signal from the optic nerves to the brain—"Oh, I see a one-yen coin"—then bend your knees, stoop, and reach out to pick it up cannot possibly be compensated for by one yen; overall, it seems to result in a deficit. Although my husband had told me about this theory before, (...) he first thought, "Oh no, I dropped one yen. It's dirty, and I don't want to pick it up," and then picked it up. Therefore, the energy consumed by that unnecessary thought must have been greater than that of someone who simply saw a one-yen coin and picked it up. Converted into money, it probably amounted to about three yen. That means a two-yen deficit.

Even so, when a one-yen coin is dropped, people usually pick it up anyway. My husband said, "The moment you see a one-yen coin lying there, it is as if you have already encountered a traffic accident. (...) A dropped one-yen coin is something whose mechanism inevitably leads to a deficit."

My husband gazed into the distance and said this, but how much energy did the act of explaining the "dropped one-yen coin" theory ultimately consume? I have a feeling that, right here in our home, where no one-yen coin has been dropped, the trouble of bringing up the story and launching into a long explanation with clever rhetoric, waving his hands and using such an extensive vocabulary, resulted in a much greater deficit.

default.p.test-45-p1.vietnamese:
A

After the Meiji Restoration, Japan decisively broke away from China—which had been the center of culture until then—raised the slogan “Leave Asia, Enter Europe,” and devoted itself to adopting European science and technology. (Omitted)

During this period, a considerable amount of new Japanese vocabulary was created. This was because model texts on European and American science had to be translated into Japanese. In other words, it became necessary to create new terms. Since these were words that existed neither in Japanese nor in Chinese characters, this must have been an extremely difficult task. (Omitted)

There are countless compounds written with kanji that originated in Japan, including the word “science” itself, as well as “physics,” “chemistry,” “molecule,” “atom,” “mass,” “solid,” “time,” “space,” “theory,” and “evolution.” In Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore, on the other hand, science classes can only be conducted in English. Japan, however, conducted science classes in Japanese from the very beginning. Science textbooks were also written in Japanese. This is truly remarkable.

B

Even today, English is still used for instruction at universities in India. Although India has Hindi as its national language, the area in which Hindi is understood is in fact limited to only part of India; in the south, people use languages belonging to the entirely different Dravidian language family. India also has many other languages, so it is said that teaching in Hindi ultimately proved impossible. Compared with languages like these, I think Japanese is an extraordinarily wonderful language.

The fact that university lectures can be given in Japanese in Japan is first of all due to the widespread use of Japanese throughout every corner of the country; therefore, any student can understand if the lecture is given in the Tokyo dialect. But that is not the whole story. Even in the Philippines and Indonesia, the technical terms used in the most advanced scientific fields do not exist in their national languages. Such terms inevitably have to be borrowed from English. Because of the reasoning that “if that is the case, we might as well not use the mother tongue at all,” it is said that they conduct all their classes in English.

default.p.test-46-p1.vietnamese:
Science and technology have greatly transformed the world in which human beings live. In other words, they have turned a world that people could neither see nor accomplish on their own into a visible world—a world of possibilities. (Excerpt) In a sense, science and technology once served as tools for making human dreams come true. It can be said that the history of science and technology is the history of human beings continually developing tools to realize their dreams and satisfy their desires.

The issue here is that the development of science and technology is cumulative. Once the bicycle made it possible to travel faster and farther, the next step was to improve it so that people could travel even faster, carry more people, or develop entirely new tools. The point we reach today becomes the starting point for the next stage. For this reason, although people may have been deeply moved when a fully automatic washing machine was first delivered to their homes, after a while it became the ordinary standard, and people began demanding even greater convenience.

This cumulative quality is not limited to science and technology; it is a common characteristic of all human cultural phenomena. Whether creating works of literature or art, authors must struggle to find themes and techniques that have never been expressed before. This is because the past has accumulated, and they begin from that foundation. Because science and technology also develop cumulatively, we have been able to amass such an enormous amount of knowledge and create extraordinarily powerful tools. (Excerpt)

However, as science continues to develop rapidly and cumulatively, its scale becomes excessively large and powerful, exceeding the limits of human imagination. When this happens, unforeseen side effects may arise, leading to accidents, or substances such as asbestos may devastate people's health without their realizing it. This is the negative side that science and technology possess today.

When this happens, science and technology, which had always been entities that realized dreams and brought hope, begin to be conspicuously viewed as threats to people's lives and health. Although problems such as environmental pollution also existed, until the 1960s and 1970s science and technology were still seen as a brilliant, rosy picture. Then, as people gradually began to worry about side effects and the international community began to examine global environmental problems, negative stereotypes and images erupted with great force in a very short time. Regarding this, although it is true that science and technology have increasingly had more negative effects, I think part of the reason is that people's admiration for their benefits became inflated, causing their sense of gratitude and appreciation to gradually fade.

default.p.test-5-p1.vietnamese:
People who are bad at keeping their rooms tidy usually own too many things. The key to tidying up is to create a "designated place" for each item. If you put things back in their designated places immediately after using them, they will no longer be scattered around the room. In addition, to make space for these designated places, it is also necessary to throw away things you do not need. Keep only an appropriate amount of belongings for your room, arranged so they are easy to see and take out. This way, you will know immediately what you are missing and can also prevent wasteful purchases, such as buying items similar to ones you already own.

((Note)) Designated place: a place or position that has been assigned.

default.p.test-51-p1.vietnamese: I think that being able to appreciate the beauty of fallen leaves may be a privilege unique to human beings. They are not beautiful simply because the leaves gradually turn yellow or red. The young leaves that emerge yellowish green in spring become deep green in summer. These brief few months are the golden period in a leaf's life. Then, when autumn arrives, the leaf changes itself into shades of red or yellow, brings its short life to an end, and falls. When I think that, with such a fragile life, the leaf has lived to the fullest amid countless colors, I cannot help feeling that it is truly beautiful. The leaf's life is exhausted at that point, but when the harsh winter ends, a new life begins on that very same tree. Life is so fragile, yet so remarkably resilient.

default.p.test-52-p1.vietnamese:
Knowing that something must be done but being unable to start it and instead doing something else is called “procrastination.” Repeated procrastination is known not only to put the outcome of an action at risk, but also to increase the likelihood of depression and anxiety disorders.

According to experts, people who tend to procrastinate have a poor ability to understand how their judgments and actions will affect them in the future. Because the ultimate goal is too far away, they cannot visualize it. For such people, it is very effective to set multiple small goals that are easy to achieve. Each time they accomplish a goal, they should reward themselves with a small reward, such as a coffee break, and then move on to the next small goal. By repeating this process, they can eventually reach the final destination.

default.p.test-53-p1.vietnamese:
In ancient times, there was no illness called hay fever.

Two hundred million years ago, when dinosaurs still existed on Earth, the first mammals appeared. However, mammals at that time are said to have suffered greatly because blood-sucking ticks clung tightly to their skin and fed on their blood. This was because they did not yet have an immune system to defend against the ticks.

During the process of evolution, however, mammals acquired a new immune system to deal with blood-sucking ticks. Random mutations also occurred at this point, and it is believed that only mammals that happened to develop an immune system capable of resisting the ticks survived.

This immune system identified the ticks as foreign objects and released substances to destroy them. As a result, mammals were able to drive away the ticks.

In a clean environment like present-day Japan, people are no longer bothered by ticks as much as they were in the past. In such circumstances, the immune system that had once fought blood-sucking ticks became a valuable but unused tool. Consequently, it began mistaking random things entering from outside for enemies and attacking them. The things mistaken for ticks were cedar pollen. When cedar pollen enters the body, the human immune system is mistakenly activated and releases substances to destroy the ticks. This causes itchy, irritated eyes and repeated sneezing.

Viewed in this way, hay fever can be understood as an illness caused by our living environment becoming excessively clean.

default.p.test-54-p1.vietnamese:
First, gather all reference materials related to the subject. Do not begin reading until you have collected as much as you possibly can. Once the materials have accumulated to the point where you can say, "This is all there is," stack them beside your desk.

Then read each book from beginning to end, one after another. If you spend time on unnecessary tasks, you will never finish reading. You may write a few short memo-like lines, but never copy anything into a notebook or make flashcards.

People who worry, "Won't I forget everything if I do that?" are notebook users or flashcard users. If you are one of them, do not imitate this method. Even if you do, you certainly will not succeed.

Memorize everything in your head. Of course, you will forget things. However, you will not forget absolutely everything, as you would if you wrote things in a notebook or on flashcards. ①It is truly strange.

（Passage omitted）

After finishing a book, ②you must write a summary as soon as possible. This is because once your enthusiasm cools, forgetting proceeds very quickly. Although you will not forget the truly important parts, small details will not necessarily remain clear forever.

When countless pieces of knowledge and facts are swirling around in your head, organizing them into a summary is not as easy as one might expect. This is because some knowledge naturally resists being condensed. However, since you have neither a notebook nor flashcards, you must finish organizing everything before the "notebook in your head" is erased by information written into it later.

Because you stack up books and read them all the way through, this can be called the ③Tsundoku method (stacking and reading). Normally, "tsundoku" means merely stacking books without reading them, but the "Tsundoku method," literally, is a study method: stack them up, then read them. And this method produces surprisingly good results.

default.p.test-55-p1.vietnamese:
In today's age, “speed reading” is attracting a great deal of attention as a way to absorb vast amounts of information in a short time. With business books as the main focus, many people believe that quickly skimming the essential points and increasing the number of books they read is the shortest path to expanding their knowledge. Indeed, this reading method is effective for quickly grasping the latest trends or getting a general understanding of the main points.

However, it is not enough to read every book quickly in the same way. In particular, when reading passages containing the author's deep ideas or complex arguments, it is essential to pause and read carefully—“close reading (Note 1)”—while comparing the text with one's own experiences and thoughts. Even if someone reads quickly by following only the surface of the words, it would be difficult to say that they have truly understood the book if they have not used their own mind to think deeply about it.

The important thing is to change one's reading style flexibly according to the purpose of reading and the nature of the text. If one is simply checking facts, dealing with them quickly is sufficient. However, if one wants to gain new perspectives and deep insight (Note 2), what is truly required is the attitude of taking time to reflect and engage in a dialogue with the text.

(Note 1) Close reading: Reading a passage carefully and thoroughly, down to the smallest details.

(Note 2) Insight: Seeing through the essence of something or what lies deep within a phenomenon.

A

In recent years, many companies have introduced internal chat tools. Because chat makes it possible to communicate work-related matters quickly without having to worry about the other person's workload, it has significantly increased the speed of information sharing. Furthermore, since past exchanges are saved in written form, it is highly effective in preventing misunderstandings about instructions and missed confirmations. To improve work efficiency and maximize individual productivity, companies should shift from traditional communication by telephone or face-to-face conversation to communication centered on chat tools.

B

Communication through chat tools is certainly convenient and fast, but I am skeptical about a work environment that relies exclusively on this medium. When people communicate only in writing, it is difficult to convey subtle nuances or emotions, which can sometimes lead to unintended misunderstandings or damage relationships. In emergencies, when discussing complex matters, or when building relationships of trust, face-to-face conversation or a telephone call—where people can listen to one another's voices—is unquestionably superior. Rather than focusing solely on efficiency, it is important to actively create opportunities for direct communication according to the specific content and circumstances.

default.p.test-57-p1.vietnamese:
In recent years, the Internet has made it possible to obtain any information in an instant, and the tendency to value “efficiency” and “the shortest route” in everything has continued to grow. In both business and education, eliminating waste thoroughly to produce results in a short time is often highly valued. It is true that using our limited time efficiently is important, and efforts to optimize efficiency in our daily work and studies are certainly not something that should be rejected.

However, might the attitude of prioritizing only answers that are easy to grasp conceal unforeseen dangers? For example, when faced with a new problem we have never encountered before, if we simply search for and copy exactly the solution someone else has provided, it is difficult to gain a thorough understanding of the basic principles or logic behind it. If we avoid the hard work of thinking things through ourselves and repeatedly going through trial and error, our superficial knowledge may increase, but we will immediately lose the ability to adapt as soon as the initial conditions or circumstances change even slightly.

Inherently, the ability to deeply understand the essence of things and create our own new perspectives is nurtured precisely through the process of “taking the long way around,” which may seem useless at first glance. The experience of stopping, holding on to our questions, and patiently searching for clues to solve a problem develops flexibility in thinking and a multifaceted perspective. The experience of thinking things through using our own abilities after overcoming repeated failures will surely become a solid foundation for surviving in this age of dramatic change.

Precisely because we live in an age convenient for pursuing efficiency, perhaps we need even more to be required not only to remain trapped by speed and immediate results, but also to consciously set aside time for deep reflection.

（(Note 1)）Harmful effects: unwanted results or negative effects.

（(Note 2)）Exploration and experimentation: searching for different ways to solve a problem.

default.p.test-58-p1.vietnamese:
At Aoba Cultural Center, we rent various conference rooms and recording studios to support cultural activities and interaction among local residents. Those wishing to use the facilities should apply at the reception desk or through the official website between 3 months and 7 days before the date of use. In addition, organizations using the facility for the first time must present identification at the reception desk and complete their application no later than 10 days before the date of use.

【Notes on Use】

Eating and drinking inside the recording studios is strictly prohibited. Guests may bring snacks or tea into the conference rooms, but each person must take any resulting waste home.

Guests may enter the room 10 minutes before the scheduled start time. However, all preparation and cleanup after use must be completed within the approved period of use.

Canceling a reservation is free of charge if done at least 7 days before the date of use. However, cancellations from 6 days before through the day before will incur 50% of the usage fee, while cancellations on the date of use will incur the full 100% cancellation fee.

When an organization consisting only of high school students or younger uses a facility, an accompanying adult responsible for the group must be present throughout the period of use (Note 1).

（(Note 1)）Accompanying: Going along beside someone.

○ When returning home and opening the door

It is very dangerous if someone realizes that you live alone. Open the door while saying『I'm home~』as if someone in your family were waiting inside. Also, ringing the doorbell before opening the door and pretending that you are visiting someone can be effective.

○ When you encounter a burglar

Suppose there is a burglar inside your room. What would you do? In an apartment building, for example, the burglar's only escape routes are the entrance or the windows. Let the burglar escape quickly, and absolutely do not chase them.

（Note 1）室内: Inside a room

（Note 2）逃げ道: A route or way of escape

default.p.test-9-p1.vietnamese:
Human beings are animals that use language. Language is a means of expressing meaning through sounds and conveying it to others, but sounds and meanings have very different qualities. Sounds are something people can perceive with their ears, whereas meanings exist only in people's minds.
